en: It was a time of blazing splendor.
The accomplished imperial Chinese
Were shaken from their foundations;
It was the hour of their onrush.
The earth trembled and swayed;
It was the hour of their onrush.
All the people drew apart.
Unbeliever and Muslim
Met face to face in the empty desert.
Riderless horses plunged and reared;
All the warriors were shattered.
The rising dust became something extraordinary.
Bakai the leopard, the revered master,
Stood as a support to Manas,
With Ajybai, son of Khan Argyn.
Renowned Manas the leopard
Placed the seven spiritual masters from Mecca
At seven separate stations.
Then your Sultan Manas
Laid low whatever place he reached.
Among the jacket-wearing Chinese,
All the strongest men
Had already been slaughtered
By the martyrs who had since died.
The remaining Black Chinese—
Manas the leopard and your Bakai
Charged them and drove them off.
The Chinese were put to flight.
The unbelievers, like black jackdaws,
Were crushed by precious Manas.
When they saw Manas’s appearance,
Helplessly they panicked:
“Manas has come back dead!”
They howled, despairing of their lives.
Unable to turn them back by raising the standard,
The Chinese could offer no resistance.
All their warriors gathered,
And countless numbers were killed.
Many a splendid khan died;
Before Manas and Bakai,
All who encountered them died.
Imperial Beijing—
The Chinese, forced upright in terror,
Were now hemmed in and driven away.
Through their center, warrior Manas
Carved a path and drove them on.
Along both flanks, warrior Bakai
Slaughtered them and drove them on.
Along the very edges, the forty companions
Slaughtered them and drove them on.
Through the very center, Khan Manas
Slaughtered them and drove them on.
All around them, his Bakai
Moved onward, hemming them in.
Those in coats who fell into their hands—
The Muslims following behind
Stripped and plundered them as they went.
The exceptionally able warriors,
When the Chinese fled toward Beijing,
All the resourceful men
Took six thousand horses apiece.
The poorer men who could not take as much
Took six hundred horses apiece.
All the accomplished men
Took seven thousand horses apiece.
The paupers who could not keep up
Took seven hundred horses apiece.
They took elephants as spoils
And loaded gold coins upon the elephants.
The champions who risked their lives
Took a thousand dark-eyed captives,
Taking the most skillful of the women.
With thimble mouths and young camels’ eyes,
From among the swaying beauties
They took some twelve thousand girls.
Noble young wives and beautiful girls—
They could not take them all as booty.
Their gold and gold coins—
The Muslims who survived the slaughter
Could no longer load them all.
They plundered their goods
And wrought such devastation.
Many a singular khan died;
Many a heroic soul died.
People marveled at the slaughter.
In red rawhide shoes and blue robes,
The Chinese people wandered in distress.
Their khans became captives;
The Chinese multitudes were slaughtered.
The sight of it brought anguish.
Named the Great Campaign,
This great slaughter that had occurred
There in imperial Beijing
Was entered into the registers.
Grieving at the mention of the slaughter,
“Until the Day of Judgment
This deed will not be forgotten,” they said.
At that time, among the Chinese,
It was inscribed in their writings.
Striking tirelessly on campaign,
They took much gold and cloth.
Not merely for warriors Almambet and Chubak,
They took blood-price worth more than the world.
Esenkan and Kongurbay,
Saying, “The lion Manas has come!”
Entered Beijing and shut themselves in,
Locking their gates,
With the many Chinese who remained.
Unable to break through the gate,
Warrior Bakai kept his regret within.
Imperial Beijing and its people—
Its gates were firm as stone.
The Flood had never swept into it;
Its people had existed since that time.
Beyond the reach of a prophet’s authority,
It was a fortress with a king.
No one could break through and take it;
Dog-cursed Beijing was secure.
On the near side of the wall
Was a trench dug forty cubits deep.
When one approached the wall,
There was boiling brine.
Stretched above the wall
Was a net spread out of iron.
No one could break through and take it;
Whoever challenged this place met misery.
Roaring the battle cry “Baltai!” in fury,
Pounding upon Beijing,
There stood mighty Manas, the Blood-Shedder.
The wall was forty cubits high;
The ditch was forty cubits deep.
When struck by an axe, it boomed.
Was it clay, or was it iron?
It roared like a war drum.
Upon its corners standing in a row,
Forty men could stand abreast.
“I shall bore through the corner,”
If someone set himself to that work,
Even if forty thousand strongmen gathered,
They would have forty years of labor.
All the warriors favored by Khizr,
If they kept coveting this place,
Daughter-damned Beijing could slaughter them.
Roaring in fury,
He embarked upon a dreadful deed.
“All together, break its gate!”
Those who had survived the deaths—
Mighty Manas, commanding them,
Had them slaughtered outright.
The precious lion who never budged—
Against the gate made of bronze
It was there he made his assault.
“I shall break its prosperous gate
Right through its middle!
Kongurbay, khan of Beijing,
I shall offer as a sacrifice!
For Almambet and Syrgak
Thus I shall take vengeance!
Upon firmly locked Beijing
I shall descend from above!
Its lord Esenkan—
I shall slaughter him and drink his blood!
For the handful of Muslims
I shall open the way this instant!
Parted from Almambet,
How can I return with eyes staring helplessly?
My companions, like twin lambs—
Parted from both at once,
How can I live on without dying?”
He struck Buurul upon the thigh.
It was the command of God.
At Beijing veiled in haze,
Turning his lacquered spear in his grip,
Your warrior thrust at this gate.
Your warrior-lion Manas thrust once
And knocked down its broad iron.
Bakai the leopard thrust once
And smashed its threshold.
Khan Ajybai thrust once
And knocked off only a teacup’s worth of earth.
Raging, the blood-shedding lion
Seized his black-cheeked battle-axe
And swung it around.
The stout gate with steel doors
He now made crash and thunder.
Dust rose from the gate.
The two khans, Ajybai and Bakai,
Felt their souls depart whenever they thought of it.
Then a voice sounded from the sky:
“Against Beijing, untouched by Chaliyar,
Your standing is insufficient: turn back!
Against Beijing, unreached by the Flood,
Your company is insufficient: turn back!
Against Beijing, untouched by Chaliyar,
Your strength is insufficient: turn back!
O warrior, if you keep matching yourself against Beijing,
Your ribs will crack and tear apart;
Your blood will pour out like dark water.
The command written by God
Is thus—see it for yourself!
Return to your own land and die there.”
As the voice sounded from the sky,
As that cry kept ringing out,
He cried, “Allah!” and withdrew from Beijing.
At the spring-fed stream of Batkaktuu,
All the holy men gathered.
They dipped their hands into water
And performed their ablutions.
Men endowed with sacred power had come;
To this imperial Beijing
Twelve pairs of khans had come.
Aykojo from Mecca had said,
“For the handful of Muslims
I shall serve as imam.”
Thus he had come to lead the prayers.
Loudly they called the call to prayer,
And gathered together.
When they came to seek their khans,
Khans Muzburchak and Kokcho were absent.
Bokmurun, son of Kokotoy,
That warrior, his only son, was absent too.
When they sought the forty companions,
Your lion Alma the leopard was absent;
Precious Chubak the wolf was absent;
Syrgak, son of Khan Ulak, was absent.
The support on which they girded themselves was gone.
Among the forty champions,
With mighty Alma at their head,
Twelve wolves were absent!
When they entered this Beijing,
It had been a road cut by Khizr.
At that time, when the Muslims
Took a count of their people,
Their army had been forty-two san.
The people’s khans were absent;
Manas grieved and sobbed.
The reason for his sobbing—
All those precious ones were gone!
In Beijing, where he had waged his campaign,
Your warrior had lost Akkula to a bullet
And sent Almambet to a martyr’s death.
His wing had been broken;
He had lost Khan Chubak, his trusted support.
He had raided Beijing and taken much;
Yet all the champions,
Through neglect, Manas had consumed!
Khans Muzburchak and Kokcho had died;
All who encountered Beijing had died.
All the mighty men—
Your warrior had let China take them as gifts!
Those who came died, souls died;
They were slaughtered in Beijing.
Warrior, all who encountered it died.
“I have the strength,” he had said as he came,
Manas the leopard, thundering.
Demanding Beijing and then turning back,
